description: HackBattle FAQ knowledge base (PRIVATE - contains organiser contact details; do not commit to a public repository).

chunks.text: About HackBattle: HackBattle is a dynamic 36-hour hackathon organised by IEEE CS as part of graVITas 2026 at VIT (Vellore Institute of Technology). Innovators, creators, and problem solvers come together to code, collaborate, and compete, turning ideas into real-world solutions. Alongside the competition there are inspiring sessions from industry leaders offering insights, guidance, and networking.

Dates, timing and duration of the event: HackBattle is a 36-hour hackathon held on 12-13 September 2026. The event starts at 8:00 am on 12 September and ends at 8:00 pm on 13 September 2026. It is an overnight coding marathon. When is the event: 12 and 13 September 2026.

Teams, team size, registration and eligibility: Team size must be 3 to 5 members. Solo participation is NOT permitted - everyone must be part of a team, and you cannot participate alone or individually as a single person. Participants can be from any background, branch or discipline. Registration (sign up) is done individually: if you register without a team, you will be placed with team members before the event begins, so you can sign up alone but you cannot compete alone. Teams must complete official registration before the event starts.

Project development rules and themes: All coding and development must happen within the 36-hour hackathon window. Pre-built projects or existing codebases are strictly prohibited. Open-source libraries, frameworks, APIs and tools are permitted with proper attribution. Projects must align with the problem statements or themes announced at the event start. Both software and hardware projects are welcome, but hardware components and devices will NOT be provided - teams must arrange their own.

Code of conduct: There is zero tolerance for plagiarism or copying code from other teams, which results in immediate disqualification. Respectful conduct is mandatory. Students must follow the VIT code of conduct. All participants must adhere to venue guidelines including safety, cleanliness, and discipline.

Logistics, venue and what to bring: A valid ID (ID card) is required for all participants. Teams must bring their own laptops, chargers, hardware components, and accessories. Internet, WiFi and basic infrastructure will be provided for on-site events. Participants must stay within the venue throughout the event unless given permission by the organizers. Meals and food breaks are provided during the hackathon.

Submissions, deadlines and how to submit: The GitHub repository link (repo link) must be shared at the beginning of the hackathon. All work must be committed to that same initial repository - no new repositories are accepted. Late submissions will NOT be accepted after the deadline. The final submission must include the complete source code in the designated repository and a documentation or README file.

General rules: Any rule violation may result in disqualification. The organizers reserve the right to modify rules, schedules, or guidelines as necessary. By participating, teams grant the organizers the right to showcase their projects on official platforms.

Evaluation criteria, judging and weightage: Projects are judged on Innovation and Creativity 25%; Technical Complexity and Implementation 25%; Problem Solving and Relevance 20%; User Experience and Design 10%; Impact and Scalability 10%; Presentation and Demonstration 10%.

Prizes and rewards: HackBattle awards a 1st Prize (first place), a 2nd Prize (second place), a 3rd Prize (third place), and a Best Freshers prize for first-year students. Prizes are given out and winners announced at the results announcement and closing ceremony on day 2.

Point of contact (POC) and contact details: The POCs for HackBattle are Aniket Bhayana (24BCE2989), phone 8861924025; Gracy Mehndiratta (24BCE2987), phone 8700945939; and Vishal Kumar Pradhwani (24BCE0766), phone 7029412141. Reach out to these organisers for queries about registration, rules, or logistics.

Classes, OD and attendance: If a participant has classes during the hackathon, they will be given OD (On Duty / on-duty attendance) for the hackathon, so attendance is covered. Registration is done individually and those without a team are placed with members before the event. Breaks will be given for meals.

Provisional schedule, day 1 (12 September 2026, times tentative): Registration and team formation 8:00-10:00 am; Opening ceremony 10:00 am (welcome, briefing, rules, introduction of judges and mentors); Development phase from 11:00 am; Lunch break 12:30-2:00 pm; Hacking resumes 2:00 pm; Speaker session 3:00-4:00 pm; Review I 4:00-7:00 pm; Dinner break 7:00-9:00 pm; Hacking 9:00 pm onward; Review 2 around 1:00-3:00 am; Ice-breaker session 3:00-4:00 am.

Provisional schedule, day 2 (13 September 2026, times tentative): Hacking continues into the morning; Review 3 around 12:00-1:00 pm; Lunch break 1:00-2:00 pm; Integration of the work 2:00-4:00 pm; Final team pitches 4:00-6:00 pm; Results announcement and closing ceremony 6:00-8:00 pm.

Tracks and themes overview: HackBattle has five tracks. Each team must select exactly ONE track. Within that track, teams may choose one or more subtracks for their project. Subtrack descriptions are ideas and possible directions only, not exhaustive or prescriptive - teams are free to explore any project that fits the broader theme of their chosen subtrack. The five tracks are: Track 1 AI and Automation; Track 2 Systems and Infrastructure; Track 3 Developer Tooling; Track 4 Cybersecurity and Privacy; Track 5 Open Innovation.

Track 1, AI and Automation track: the AI and Automation track challenges teams to rescue AI from the chat window - give it hands, memory, and a sense of boundaries so it can interact with the real world without constant supervision. Subtracks of the AI and Automation track: Agentic Workflows (AI that can plan, trigger external APIs, and execute multi-step tasks autonomously); Self-Learning and Adaptation (models that keep learning as the underlying data changes, adapting to new patterns without retraining from scratch); Guardrails and Trust (filters, evaluation harnesses, or honeypots that keep model outputs safe, accurate and aligned).

Track 2, Systems and Infrastructure: The challenge is to engineer the invisible plumbing - tools that make deploying code faster, networks more resilient, or data syncing seamless when the connection drops. Subtracks: Cloud and Deployment Automation (scripts or platforms that remove manual server management and automate release cycles); Decentralization and Protocols (peer-to-peer file sharing, custom network layers, localized communication tools, custom proxies, or tools that keep data flowing when the connection drops); Core Systems and Data Engines (lightweight caching systems, fast data synchronizers, custom local storage engines, or OS-level work such as system utilities and micro-schedulers).

Track 3, Developer Tooling: The challenge is to build the tools you wish you had at 3 AM when your codebase was on fire. Subtracks: Terminal and Shell Tooling (command-line utilities, shell enhancements, scripting frameworks, or custom dev-environment plugins); Codebase Intelligence and Navigation (assistants, AI or algorithmic, that help engineers understand and move through large codebases - dependency mappers, semantic code search, refactoring aids, or repo-wide Q&A tools); Workflow and Context Management (tools that eliminate context-switching, such as workspace orchestrators, smart snippet managers, or local automation engines).

Track 4, Cybersecurity and Privacy track: the cybersecurity track challenges teams to lock down the digital ecosystem - protect the user, assume the network is already hostile, or expose invisible data-harvesting. Subtracks of the Cybersecurity and Privacy track: Local-First Privacy (applications where sensitive data never leaves the device, such as offline password managers, private on-device AI assistants, or encrypted personal knowledge bases); Defense and Sandboxing (systems treating every application, file and network as untrusted by default - browser sandboxing tools, suspicious file detonation environments, permission-aware firewalls, malware analysis sandboxes); Surveillance Transparency (browser extensions, local proxies, or analysis tools that expose hidden telemetry and show what a site is harvesting, from shadow cookies to ETag tracking).

Track 5, Open Innovation: If none of the other tracks appeal, this is the open playground to build something completely new. Teams can wire up Hardware and IoT, work with AR/VR, explore Web3, craft an immersive game, or build something that defies categories. This track has NO fixed subtracks and teams are free to choose their own path.

What is IEEE CS VIT: IEEE CS VIT is the IEEE Computer Society student chapter at Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), and is the organiser of HackBattle. Founded in 2012, IEEE CS VIT operates as part of IEEE Region 10 and the Madras Section. IEEE CS VIT is a student-driven technology community focused on computer science and emerging technologies, where members learn, experiment, collaborate and build practical solutions. IEEE CS VIT is not merely an event-organizing club: its identity also includes technical project development, experimentation, collaboration and practical technology education.

What IEEE CS VIT does: its activities cover building technology projects; organizing technical events and competitions such as hackathons, cybersecurity challenges, coding competitions and machine-learning competitions; conducting workshops and learning initiatives; working on real-world technical problems; collaborating with external organizations; and giving students opportunities to develop practical technical skills. Areas of activity include software development, artificial intelligence and machine learning, web and application development, cybersecurity, and competitive programming.

IEEE CS VIT projects overview: the chapter has five notable projects - the Kalaburagi Airport Project with the Airports Authority of India; the Financial Insights Analyzer and Summarizer with the NFRA; Chota Dhobi, a hostel laundry app; the Pravega Racing web app; and AssignoFast, a student academic task manager. Some are developed by IEEE CS VIT and others are collaborations or external competition entries.

Kalaburagi Airport Project: IEEE CS VIT collaborated with the Airports Authority of India (AAI) on a technology project to modernize and streamline airport operations and services. The work involved Management Information Systems (MIS) and Multimodal Transport Systems. This was an external, industry-facing collaboration involving airport infrastructure and transportation management.

Financial Insights Analyzer and Summarizer: IEEE CS VIT worked on this project in collaboration with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). It focused on analyzing financial information and generating summarized insights. IEEE CS VIT entered it at Techkriti, the annual technical festival of IIT Kanpur, where it secured 2nd place and a prize of Rs 1,00,000. This was an external competition and collaboration rather than an internal application.

Chota Dhobi: a laundry-management application developed by IEEE CS VIT for VIT hostels. It was designed to make hostel laundry operations more organized and efficient for students. According to IEEE CS VIT, the application served approximately 50,000 users. This is an example of an IEEE CS VIT-developed application deployed within the VIT ecosystem.

Pravega Racing web app: IEEE CS VIT collaborated with Pravega Racing to help develop its web application. The app was built to give the racing team a fast, responsive and visually polished web experience, with an emphasis on accessibility and global connectivity. This was a collaborative development project rather than a project owned entirely by IEEE CS VIT.

AssignoFast: a student productivity and academic task-management system developed by IEEE CS VIT. It helps students manage assignments, deadlines, timetables and academic tasks in one place. Capabilities include synchronization of assignments from VTOP, timetable synchronization, assignment and deadline tracking, notifications and reminders, personal task management, support for Moodle quizzes, a Chrome extension and a mobile application. It is designed around the academic workflow of VIT students.

IIT Bombay Techfest first place: IEEE CS VIT built a Hybrid Voice Security System that fuses Wav2Vec 2.0 with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) and Graph Attention to detect complex deepfake artifacts. The microservice was integrated into a VLM-driven agentic framework enabling secure transactions. This won first place at IIT Bombay Techfest.
